subject: probability-and-statistics
subtopics: the random variable as a function from the sample space to the real line, and the discrete against the continuous case
the probability distribution, the probability mass function for a discrete variable, the density for a continuous one, and the cumulative distribution function
normalising a density or a mass function, and computing the probability of an interval
the expectation of a discrete and of a continuous random variable, and linearity
the variance and the standard deviation, with Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2
the Bernoulli trial and the binomial distribution: mass function, mean np and variance np(1-p)
the Poisson distribution: mass function, mean equal to variance, and its origin in a Poisson process
the exponential distribution: density, survival function, mean 1/lambda and memorylessness
the continuous uniform distribution: density, mean, variance and the ratio-of-lengths rule
the normal distribution: density, the parameters mu and sigma, standardisation, symmetry and the empirical rule
choosing the distribution a word problem describes
sums of independent random variables and the reproductive property

chosen.title: Lecture 13: Random Variables
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: the random variable as a function from outcomes to numbers
the measurability condition
the motivation for quantifying an experiment
chosen.why: The clearest English statement of what a random variable is and why the definition needs measurability, read from its opening through the inverse-image condition. Chosen over a formula list because the card that teaches the definition needs the reason, not the symbol.

chosen.title: Lecture 15: Probability Distribution of a Random Variable - II
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: the mass function worked on a small example
the definition of a continuous variable through its CDF
the density as the derivative of the CDF
the two conditions on a density
chosen.why: The only source read this run that defines the continuous random variable through an absolutely continuous CDF and then derives the density from it, which is exactly the chain the CDF and normalisation cards need. Its four-bulb worked example is also the smallest honest example of a PMF found.

chosen.title: Lecture 19: Special Discrete Distributions - I
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: the discrete uniform distribution with its mean and variance
the degenerate distribution
the Bernoulli trial
chosen.why: Supplies the discrete-uniform formulas that the uniform card uses as a contrast, and the Bernoulli setup that opens the binomial card, both derived term by term rather than quoted.

chosen.title: Lecture 20: Special Discrete Distributions - II
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: a binomial application solved end to end
the geometric distribution
the negative binomial
chosen.why: The airline overbooking example is a full binomial computation with a complement, which is the pattern GATE's 'exactly k out of n' questions use; it is the only readable worked binomial problem found this run.

chosen.title: Lecture 21: Special Discrete Distributions - III
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: why sampling without replacement breaks the constant-p assumption
the hypergeometric mass function
chosen.why: The binomial card states the boundary of the model - without replacement the count is not binomial - and this is the source that teaches it, with the changing probability computed explicitly at each draw.

chosen.title: Lecture 22: Poisson Process - I
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: the three assumptions of a Poisson process
the derivation of the Poisson mass function
the rescaling of the rate to the window
chosen.why: Chosen for the derivation and for the worked example in which lambda t = 15 is used for a three-minute window at 5 per minute, which is the rescaling step GATE questions punish.

chosen.title: Lecture 24: Special Continuous Distributions - I
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: the uniform density fixed by normalisation
mean (a+b)/2
variance (b-a)^2/12 and the standard deviation
chosen.why: Derives the uniform mean and variance from first principles, including the standard deviation (b-a)/(2 sqrt 3), so the uniform card's numbers are traced to an integral rather than quoted from a table.

chosen.title: Lecture 25: Special Continuous Distributions - II
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: the exponential as the waiting time of a Poisson process
memorylessness derived from the survival function
the mean 1/lambda
chosen.why: The only readable source that derives memorylessness rather than asserting it, and it states the analogy with the geometric distribution that makes the property believable.

chosen.title: Lecture 29: Normal Distribution
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: the normal density and its two parameters
standardisation
the vanishing of the odd central moments by symmetry
chosen.why: Gives the density, the standardisation and the symmetry argument that the 2008 question turns on, in one sequence. It is the same course as the other chosen lectures, so the notation is consistent across cards.

chosen.title: Probability and Statistics - lecture list
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Probability and Statistics (IIT Kharagpur, Prof. Somesh Kumar)
covers: the teaching order of the course
chosen.why: Used only to confirm that the twelve subtopics enumerated for this topic follow a standard teaching order, and to find the lecture numbers for the distributions. No content claim rests on it.

chosen.title: Lecture 30: sums of independent variables and the reproductive property
chosen.channel: NPTEL, Introduction to Probability Theory and Stochastic Processes (IIT Delhi, Prof. S. Dharmaraja)
covers: the sum of independent Poissons is Poisson
binomial and normal are closed under addition
Bernoulli is not
chosen.why: A second course, deliberately, so the sums card is not built on the same lecturer's voice as every other card. It derives the Poisson closure and states explicitly which families are and are not closed.

chosen.title: GATE Overflow for GATE CSE Volume 1 - Engineering Mathematics: Probability
covers: the distribution summaries with means and variances
the GATE pitfall list
the linearity and variance conditions
chosen.why: The GATE-oriented source: it is the only readable text this run that frames each family as a GATE pitfall list (rate against mean, variance against standard deviation, Var(X-Y), independence). Read in part through the search service's extract, and every claim taken from it is one of those framed warnings.

chosen.title: Introductory Statistics 2e, section 5.3: The Exponential Distribution
covers: the decay parameter m = 1/mu
the standard deviation equals the mean
memorylessness
the Poisson-exponential relationship
chosen.why: An independent standard text for the exponential card, used to corroborate the parameter convention (rate versus mean) and the fact that the median lies below the mean, both of which are common traps.

chosen.title: Introductory Statistics 2e, section 5.2: The Uniform Distribution
covers: the density 1/(b-a)
mean (a+b)/2 and standard deviation (b-a)/sqrt(12)
the rectangle-area method
percentiles
chosen.why: Corroborates the uniform formulas against a text independent of the NPTEL course, and supplies the rectangle-area reading that the 2019 question needs before any algebra.

chosen.title: Praayikta bantan: maadhy, prasaran, dvipad bantan
covers: the random variable as a rule
the two distribution-table rules
the balance-point reading of E(X)
Var(X) = E(X^2) - mu^2 and the E(aX+b), Var(aX+b) rules
the binomial and Poisson summaries
four common mistakes
chosen.why: The only non-English source that could be read this run, and it is worth its place: its list of four common mistakes is the source of three of this topic's trap alerts. Everything taken from it is rendered in English and the three cards that use it say so.

chosen.title: Applied Mathematics, chapter 4: Probability Distributions
covers: the definition of a random variable
discrete against continuous
the expectation and variance definitions
the four Bernoulli-trial conditions
the binomial, Poisson and normal definitions
chosen.why: A school-level Indian text, which is what the default beginner has actually met before. Chosen for the clean four-condition statement of Bernoulli trials and for the mean-median-mode equality of the normal.

chosen.title: Note on the Poisson Distribution

the proof that it sums to 1
mean nu and standard deviation sqrt(nu)
chosen.why: A short standard derivation, independent of the NPTEL course, used to verify the Poisson card's claim that the mean and the variance are the same parameter, and to check that the mass function integrates to 1.

standard_refs: Sheldon Ross, A First Course in Probability, chapters 4 to 5 (random variables, expectation, special distributions) - the book GATE preparation pages recommend for this subject
William Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, volume 1, chapters 6 and 9 (the binomial and the Poisson)
Ronald E. Walpole, Raymond H. Myers, Sharon L. Myers and Keying Ye, Probability and Statistics for Engineers and Scientists, chapters 5 to 6

GATE 2027 CS syllabus, Engineering Mathematics line 'Random variables. Uniform, normal, exponential, Poisson and binomial distributions. Mean, median, mode and standard deviation. Conditional probability and Bayes theorem.'
notes: The syllabus names this topic in one line, so the twelve subtopics above are this run's enumeration from the standard treatment (Ross chapters 4-5, the CBSE chapter 4 sequence, and the NPTEL course order 13-30), not a quotation from the syllabus. The line's own words - random variables, and the uniform, normal, exponential, Poisson and binomial distributions - each get a card, and the CDF, expectation and variance are included because every one of the ten verified questions needs at least one of them.

Ten GATE CSE previous-year questions were verified for this topic, one for each distribution the syllabus names plus the CDF, the expectation and the identification of a family: 2006 Q.21 (binomial), 2008 Q.29 (normal), 2012 Q.21 (CDF), 2013 Q.2 (Poisson), 2017 Set 2 Q.48 (Poisson moments), 2019 Q.47 (uniform), 2021 Set 1 Q.18 (exponential), 2025 Set 1 Q.48 (density normalisation), 2026 Set 1 Q.48 (expectation) and 2026 Set 2 Q.4 (normal identification).

Every PYQ is SOURCED against a GATE Overflow accepted answer, not key-verified against an official answer key: the official papers and keys were not fetched this run, so no marks field is recorded and every question reference follows the GATE Overflow numbering. Where another site numbers the question differently the record says so.

No video transcript was readable this run, so no card quotes or timestamps a lecture and videoRefs is empty on every card. The lectures cited are NPTEL transcripts served as PDFs, read from their opening to the point named in each source note - PARTIAL, not full.

The only non-English source is a Hindi page on probability distributions, marked translated on the three cards that use it. No Hindi, Tamil, Telugu or Bengali lecture could be read, and no card quotes a Hindi sentence: what is used is the page's structure, its four-mistake list and its formulas, all rendered in English.

The sums-of-independent-variables card is P3 and carries no PYQ: no verified CSE question in this topic is decided by the reproductive property alone. It is included because it is the fact that makes several distractor options wrong, and the card says plainly that it is not a PYQ pattern.

The choosing-the-right-distribution card is P2 and carries no PYQ of its own: it is the decision that opens every one of the ten verified questions, so its evidence is the ten questions rather than one.
